name: The distinctive character of scientific authority
plain_explanation: Unlike the Church, which demanded belief on pain of punishment and claimed a complete, eternally fixed system covering all of morality and history, science persuades only by appeal to reason, covers only a small 'island' of what has been ascertained, and holds its conclusions tentatively, as probable rather than certain.
precise_definition: Russell's contrast: ecclesiastical authority is governmental, total, and dogmatically certain; scientific authority is 'piecemeal and partial,' intellectual rather than coercive, and 'made tentatively, on a basis of probability,' producing 'a temper of mind very different from that of the medieval dogmatist.'
why_it_mattered: This distinction explains why science, despite lacking coercive power, nonetheless displaced the Church as the dominant intellectual authority of the modern age.
historical_origin: Emerges alongside the rise of experimental and mathematical science in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
examples: Science pronounces only on 'whatever, at the time, appears to have been scientifically ascertained'
competing_positions: Catholic dogma's claim to lay down 'a complete system, covering human morality, human hopes, and the past and future history of the universe'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly contrasted with ecclesiastical governmental authority.
